strings.text: This self-contained edition requires JavaScript for its reading tools, navigation and search. It does not download scripts or send your notes anywhere. The source package includes every profile in the human-readable file src/catalogue.json.
A field guide, not a fixed itinerary.
A FIELD GUIDE TO MATHEMATICAL MINDS
Meet the people behind the proofs. Understand a breakthrough, trace a connection, and find the question that keeps you reading.
ONE QUESTION. MANY WAYS TO THINK.
From one profile to a larger idea.
Start anywhere. Your place, notes and read marks stay on this device.
FOLLOW A CONNECTION, NOT A CHECKLIST
Choose any two people and find a route through the atlas. Every step keeps its explanation attached.
Find an unread profile in a field you care about. Suggestions come from this collection, not a live feed.
Not sure whose name to look for? Follow a question across fields. These lenses index the existing profile text, rather than asserting a historical genealogy.
Every matching profile includes its own references. These are thematic reading indexes, not exhaustive surveys of a research area.
These routes organize the existing collection. Enter anywhere, skip a step, or follow a connection out of the path. Nothing here sets a daily schedule.
All 131 people, arranged by birth year—not discovery date. Ancient dates marked “c.” are approximate; ideas do not develop in one straight line.
An independent collection of mathematical lives and ideas. Built to read, revisit and connect—not to send you down a predetermined sequence.

The collection contains 131 distinct profiles, including 49 expanded articles and 82 quick portraits; 181 labeled connections; nine research fields; and eight optional reading paths. The original 118-profile source is retained unchanged; validated publication records add new articles and corrections. The shorter portraits are introductions, not complete biographies.

Open a profile, adjust its type size or line spacing, and use Focus to hide the surrounding navigation. The contents highlight your position as you scroll. A reading position is not a completion mark: only the Mark as read button changes your read list. Continue from Discover or the Recent shelf.

Every article section has its own shareable link. Equations open in a larger view with copyable plain text and, where it exists in the source, TeX. The pre-rendered mathematics needs no network connection.

The original catalogue is preserved. Editorial notes expand selected connections with sources and labels distinguishing documented relationships, mathematical connections, and thematic comparisons. Other links retain their original descriptions. The route finder searches only those recorded edges. Exploring an arrow in reverse is explicitly identified and does not reverse its historical meaning.

The 13 idea lenses include illustrated explanations and thematic bridges; their profile lists and question suggestions use text matching in this catalogue. They are navigation aids, not generated answers, scientific classifications or exhaustive literature surveys.
The starting point is the September 2026 educational snapshot. The original catalogue is preserved in the source, and subsequent changes are recorded in the

. A scheduled profile becomes part of this edition only after its update record is accepted, built and deployed. This page does not itself fetch your conversations or generate new articles. Neither the redesign nor a deployment constitutes independent re-verification of every claim.
Publishing and your private notebook are separate
. Accepted source changes can be built and deployed to GitHub Pages. New content appears after reloading the site; there is no background polling or upload of your notebook.

Notes, saved profiles and preferences remain in browser storage. There are no accounts, trackers, remote fonts, background requests or cloud uploads. Storage restrictions, private browsing, a new file location or clearing browser data can prevent your shelf from carrying over. Use a JSON backup when moving editions; Markdown export makes notes readable outside the website.
The original storage key and profile IDs are unchanged. Old JSON backups can be merged without discarding your current notes. Replace mode is available only after confirmation.

All main actions have keyboard controls, visible focus indicators and text labels. The graph has an equivalent connection list, so dragging is never necessary for exploring its data. Dialogs support Escape and return focus to the opening control. Reduced-motion preferences are respected. A manual screen-reader audit has not been performed.
One HTML file. No build step to read it. Only opening external sources needs internet.

Move between links and controls. Map nodes work with Enter or Space; the adjacent list offers the same connections without using the map.
Scrolling remembers the current article section. Use Continue on Discover or Resume in the Recent shelf to return. Mark as read is always a separate, deliberate action.
Notes save as you type. Back up the shelf as JSON to transfer it between browsers or file locations. Export your notebook as Markdown to use it in other writing tools.
Text matching and recommendations run locally. Nothing here alters a scheduled task.
New profiles and corrections, with a permanent record of what was added. Your private reading notebook is not part of this log.
A public content record is validated and rebuilt into this site. Reload after a deployment to see new content. This page never reads your ChatGPT conversations itself.
Notes and reading progress stay in browser storage. When moving from a downloaded file to the hosted site, export your old JSON backup and import it using Merge.

A mathematical model of computation. One machine can simulate the description of another. Encoding programs as data makes universality and diagonal arguments possible.

Proof without disclosure. A simulator without the secret witness must reproduce the verifier's view in the specified sense. Security against arbitrary verifiers is stronger than merely simulating an honest transcript.

IDEA LENS / Local views, global structure
The locality of first-order logic. Bounded logical depth limits the scale of local inspection. It does not mean that first-order truth is determined solely by frequencies seen from a random vertex.
Existence through randomness. For a nonnegative integer-valued X, expectation below one forces an outcome with no counted defects. This turns a probability estimate into an existence proof.

Interaction reaches polynomial space. A polynomial-time verifier can check a polynomial-space computation through randomized interaction with an unlimited prover. The theorem concerns verification, not efficient computation of the answer alone.
Symmetry becomes an algorithm. A large symmetry group can be represented by generators and studied through its actions. Large automorphism groups alone do not make an isomorphism instance hard.
Counting, circuits and learning. For a zero–one bipartite adjacency matrix, the permanent counts perfect matchings. Computing it is #P-complete under polynomial-time counting reductions.
A repetition code: 1 information bit / 3 transmitted bits
Information becomes a quantity. Entropy measures average information under a distribution. For an independent identically distributed source, it controls asymptotic lossless compression rates.
The first observer can simulate the second.
Geometry beyond flat space. A metric can vary from point to point. This permits intrinsic geometry on manifolds and later became essential to general relativity.
Algorithms with invariants. With nonnegative edge weights, the closest unsettled vertex can be finalized safely. The proof invariant is as important as the implementation.

Data structures that adapt, with proofs. Splay trees make adaptation part of the algorithm: accessing a key changes the tree. Amortized and competitive analysis explain what this simple rule guarantees, and which stronger forms of optimality remain conjectural.
Read marks, not just opened pages.

Certificates, axioms and algebra. Over an algebraically closed field, a finite polynomial system with no common zero admits this Nullstellensatz certificate. Existence of a certificate does not guarantee that it is small.
The limits of formal proof. Logical completeness concerns truth in all models. Arithmetic incompleteness concerns what a particular effectively axiomatized consistent theory can decide.
The first universal NP problem. Cook–Levin establishes a starting point for NP-completeness. The theorem does not prove that SAT requires superpolynomial time.
A network of hard problems. A polynomial-time reduction transfers an efficient algorithm for B into one for A. Starting with Cook–Levin, reductions made hardness reusable across mathematical domains.
Computation described by logic. Inductive counting can certify non-reachability in logarithmic space. On ordered finite structures, fixed-point logic also captures polynomial-time computation.

The power of separated provers. A polynomial-time verifier can cross-check separated provers about an exponentially large claimed computation. Noncommunication constrains coordinated cheating strategies.

The sharp edge of approximation. For clauses with three distinct variables, a random assignment satisfies each with probability 7/8. Beating the corresponding approximation threshold is NP-hard, up to any fixed positive slack.

A conjecture that reorganized a field. A permutation constraint determines one label from the other. The conjecture concerns distinguishing nearly satisfiable systems from systems of very low optimum, not exact satisfiability.

Fourier analysis on the Boolean cube. Fourier coefficients encode how a function depends on its coordinates. Noise stability and influence connect these coefficients to learning, PCPs and approximation.

A unified theory of CSP approximation. The theorem concerns fixed finite-domain, bounded-arity maximum CSPs and asymptotic approximation guarantees. It is not a claim that SDP solves every optimization problem exactly.

Optimization through moments. A low-degree pseudoexpectation satisfies selected consistency and positivity conditions without necessarily coming from a real distribution. Higher levels impose stronger conditions at greater cost.
Algebraic structures in their own right. Every group acts faithfully on itself by left multiplication. Cayley's theorem makes an abstract group concrete as a group of permutations.

Refining the information in a graph. Vertex color refinement is an isomorphism invariant, not a complete test. Equally sized regular graphs already show that local aggregation can miss global differences.
Sparsity with structural meaning. For bounded expansion, this bound applies to every depth-r shallow minor H. Sparse structure remains sparse after bounded-radius contractions.

Randomness with memory of the present. A transition matrix turns long-term random behavior into a problem in probability and linear algebra. Markov chains are central to sampling and randomized algorithms.

Probability from axioms. For pairwise disjoint events, countable additivity organizes probability into measure theory. His separate complexity notion measures the length of the shortest effective description.

Probability, symmetry and discovery. Return probabilities decay at a rate whose sum diverges in dimensions one and two. His enumeration theorem separately turns symmetry counting into cycle-index algebra.
Discrete questions, richer spaces. The theta function bridges an intractable combinatorial quantity and semidefinite optimization. It also gives a multiplicative upper bound for Shannon capacity.
Randomness for limited memory. A distribution can fool a resource-bounded observer without being truly uniform. The observer model and error parameter determine the required seed length.

Hardness can replace randomness. The hypothesis is a sufficiently strong circuit lower bound for an efficiently describable function, not merely P≠NP. Enumerating logarithmic-length seeds then gives deterministic simulation.
Symmetry explains solvability. A polynomial's hidden symmetries govern which algebraic operations can recover its roots. The approach made group theory central to algebra.
Structure and symmetry. Noether's theorem applies under precise variational hypotheses. Her separate algebraic work made rings, ideals and modules central organizing objects.
A new language for geometry. A scheme retains information, including infinitesimal structure, that an ordinary set of solutions may lose. This framework transformed arithmetic geometry.

Lower bounds and their barriers. If a restricted circuit admits a low-complexity approximation that the target function cannot admit, the circuit must be large. Restrictions on the circuit model are essential.
Logic becomes algebra. Boolean algebra eventually became a foundation of digital circuit design. Shannon supplied the explicit engineering bridge to switching circuits.
Secrets over a public channel. The shared algebraic value is easy for participants to obtain but should be hard for an observer to recover under the chosen group's computational assumptions.
Public-key cryptography. The algebraic identity alone is not security. Parameter choices, protocols and computational assumptions determine whether an implementation is secure.
Public-key algorithms. A public transformation can be easy to apply while reversal requires secret information or a hard computation. Bare algebraic RSA is not a complete secure encryption protocol.
Programs before electronic computers. Her importance lies in the conception and explanation of programmable symbolic machinery. The Analytical Engine itself was not completed in her lifetime.
From machine instructions to languages. Higher-level languages separate what a program expresses from one machine's instruction set. This made programming accessible at a much larger scale.

High-level programming. An effective high-level language can express scientific computation while allowing compilation to efficient machine code. Language design itself became a serious theoretical discipline.

Programs as mathematical claims. A Hoare triple expresses that, when C terminates from a state satisfying P, the resulting state satisfies Q. Termination requires additional reasoning for total correctness.
Meaning for recursive programs. A recursive specification is a fixed-point equation. Suitable ordered structures allow a least solution to be built from increasing approximations.
Types, proofs and communication. Concurrent processes interact rather than execute as one sequential thread. His formalisms let researchers reason systematically about communication and behavior.

A language for mathematical proof. An axiomatic theory distinguishes its assumptions from what follows logically. Euclid's architecture of proof became an intellectual reference point for later geometry and foundations.
Geometry in coordinates. Coordinates allow geometric questions to become algebraic calculations. This bridge underlies much of calculus, linear algebra and mathematical modeling.
Arithmetic, geometry and precision. Modular arithmetic isolates the structure of remainders. Gauss's work gave later number theory both foundational results and a standard of conceptual precision.
Shape and dynamics. The fundamental group records how loops can wind through a space. It translates a geometric problem into an algebraic invariant.
Three-dimensional geometry. A complicated manifold can be studied through canonical pieces carrying geometric structures. Perelman's later work completed geometrization via Ricci flow.
Topology through geometric flow. Ricci flow evolves a metric according to curvature. Understanding its singularities and surgery lets one extract topological information.

The geometry of all surfaces. For a fixed closed hyperbolic surface of genus g≥2, suitable counts of simple closed geodesics have polynomial asymptotics. The constant depends on the surface and counting convention.
